Abstract Keywords ► Noonan syndrome ► Kabuki syndrome ► Silver–Russell syndrome ► MLPA ► NGS Syndromes causing short stature include Noonan syndrome (NS), Williams syndrome, and Silver–Russell syndrome (SRS).
SRS is a primordial dwarﬁsm with genetic heterogeneity.
The SRS children present with prenatal growth retardation, neonatal hypoglycemia, feeding difﬁculties, physical asymmetry, with scoliosis and cardiac defect in some cases.
The incidence is up to 1 in 100,000.
Uniparental disomy, methylation abnormalities, and variants in some genes have been found underlying such phenotype.
Growth hormone therapy has been used to improve the height gain in these patients.
NS has genetic heterogeneity and most patients present with short stature with or without cardiac defect.
Multiple genetic variants, mostly autosomal dominant, contribute to the phenotype.

With the availability of nextgeneration sequencing, more and more genetic disorders causing short stature are being identiﬁed in different ethnic populations like Kabuki syndrome and Nance–Horan syndrome.
Here, we present some cases of SRS and other additional syndromes with dysmorphism seen in past 5 years.
Introduction Several genetic syndromes causing short stature are considered rare.
Relatively common ones seen in the genetic clinic are Williams syndrome (WS, OMIM # 194050) and Noonan syndrome (NS).
There are several causes of prenatal and postnatal growth retardation.
These disorders are included under the term “primordial dwarﬁsm.” 1,2
In Silver–Russell syndrome (SRS), the head circumference is relatively preserved and additional ﬁndings include body asymmetry, hypoglycemia, and feeding difﬁculties.1
Few of these patients also have a cardiac defect.
Maternal uniparental disomy (UPD) of chromosome 16 or UPD (16)mat and UPD(7) mat have been described in some of the patients.
Hypomethylation of chromosome 11p15 has been found in over 50% of the cases.
Recently, mutations in IGF2, CDKN1C, and PLAG1 have also been described in patients with such phenotype.3 NS was ﬁrst identiﬁed as one of the syndromes with Turner syndrome stigmata.

However, with further advancements in diagnostic technologies, the genetic heterogeneity and vari- able presentations are being increasingly identiﬁed.4,5 Certain syndromes with short stature can be Xlinked, and these include Nance–Horan syndrome (NHS; OMIM # 302350) and faciogenital dysplasia (FGD; OMIM # 305400).6,7 We report children with SRS and few other syndromes like Kabuki syndrome (KS) and FGD, seen in the genetic clinic of a tertiary care center.

Methods This is a retrospective analysis of syndromes presenting with short stature seen in genetic clinic and genetic ward of a tertiary care center during a 5 year period from January 2016 to October 2020.
Of total of 70 cases, 10 cases of WS and 38 cases of mucopolysaccharidoses were excluded from the detailed analysis (►Fig. 1).

Further investigations like karyotyping, methylationsensitive multiplex ligation probe ampliﬁcation (MSMLPA), or nextgeneration sequencing (NGS) were done as per further requirement depending on the clinical diagnosis.
Karyotyping was done for suspected Turner syndrome, especially females with unexplained short stature.
FISH or chromosomal microarray was done in suspected WS.
MSMLPA was performed in those with prenatal and postnatal growth retardation where SRS was suspected.
Subsequently, NGS was done; or if NS or KS was suspected from facial dysmorphic features/facial gestalt.
Genetic testing was done with proper pretest counseling and informed consent.
Clearance for publication was through the departmental review board.

The data prioritization, ﬁltering, and reporting on NGS were done as per standard American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) guidelines.8 Results Of 70 cases of short stature, there were 49 males and 21 females.
The relatively common chromosomal syndromes seen were WS and Turner syndrome.
The other syndromes and disorders included mucopolysaccharidosis that was the largest group, followed by SRS and NS.

Examination revealed mild coarse facies with pallor, generalized swelling over the body and dry hyperpigmented scales on limbs and trunk with relative sparing of the face (►Fig. 5).
His weight was 10 kg (–4.67 zscore), height was 80 cm (–6.92 zscore), and head circumference of 46.5 cm (–4.7 z).
He had cardiomegaly, liver of 3 cm below the right costal margin, mild ascites and decreased tone in the limbs.
Echocardiography showed pericardial effusion.
The thyroid proﬁle was 0.19 ng/ml, 0.42 μg/dl, and 378.8 μIU/ml units for T3, T4, TSH, respectively.
The thyroid peroxidase antibody level was 379.8 IU/ml and ultrasonography of thyroid showed hypoechoic and mildly bulky thyroid lobes.
He received supportive therapy for respiratory distress, hydrocortisone, and thyroxine supplements.
A pericardiocentesis was done to drain small amount of the pericardial ﬂuid.

The dysmorphic features were evident after the edema subsided and the features included hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral ﬁssures strabismus, dysplastic, and low set anteverted ears and short neck.
A ﬁnal diagnosis of NS with hypothyroidism with ichthyosis was made on basis of NS diagnostic criteria.

Discussion There are several genetic causes of short stature, including Turner syndrome, WS, SRS, velocardiofacial syndrome, and NS.

NS is associated mostly with pulmonic stenosis and in most cases the underlying cause is PTPN11 mutations, though multiple genes have been implicated in causation of phenotype.4,5,10 SRS has been described as a disorder of abnormal methylation and imprinting.
In up to 10% cases UPD (16)mat or UPD(7)mat have been identiﬁed.1,2

Nowadays, it is possible to identify hypomethylation of the H19DMR region by using MSMLPA or NGSbased techniques in 50 to 60% cases.9,11In one of the cases in present report, we also found hypomethylation in the region.

Based on clinical criteria also, one can diagnose SRS as elucidated in the Netchine–Harbison criteria as listed in ►Table 1.1,9 Points 1 to 6 in ►Table 1 are the clinical diagnostic criteria for SRS, which include four objective and two subjective criteria.
The body asymmetry can be conﬁrmed by measurement of limb length and limb girth in the patients using standard guidelines.
In few cases, whole body on one side may be smaller, called hemihypotrophy.
Xrays can help in diagnosis of hip dysplasia.
History of neonatal hypoglycemia may also be found in SRS patients.
The differential diagnosis includes 3M syndrome, FloatingHarbor syndrome, and SHORT syndrome; the ﬁrst two also cause primordial dwarﬁsm.12 Fig.

SHORT refers to constellation of ﬁndings in addition to short stature, including also hyperextensibility of joints /hernias, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and delay in teething.
In these syndromes, joint hypermobility or joint laxity is usually observed.
Relative macrocephaly also occurs in 3M syndrome.
MLPA not only helps in conﬁrmation of diagnosis but also in cases of suspected WS, and MSMLPA can diagnose Prader–Willi syndrome.

Methylation disorders like SRS and BeckwithWeidemann syndrome (BWS) are more likely to be seen in children born of assisted reproductive technologies, and MSMLPA can help in diagnosing both.11 Hypermethylation of H19DMR region occurs in BWS.

The presence of mildto-moderate microcephaly and digital anomalies is highly suggestive of a diagnosis of Feingold syndrome.

The variant found in the child in ►Table 2— FGD1: deletion of xon 9–18, has been described as likely pathogenic in an earlier report.15 In NHS, there are mutations in NHS gene on short arm of X chromosomeXp22.2p22.1.
Lens opacities are seen in 90% of heterozygous males—lens opacities involve posterior Ysutures.
The other ocular abnormalities are microphthalmia, microcornea, and strabismus; and most affected males have signiﬁcant visual impairment.
The NHS protein colocalizes with a tight junction protein in the cell membrane of epithelial cells and is involved in cataractogenesis.6
A nonsense hemizygous variant was observed—NHS:c.666C > A:p.(Cys222(cid:4))—in the 7year-old patient in present series (►Table 2).

In a family with multiple affected members of an Indian family with severe ocular ﬁndings, another truncating mutation NHS: c.115C > T:p.(Gln39(cid:4)) has been described earlier.16 Postnatal growth failure with endocrine abnormalities is also seen in defects of DNA repair mechanism involving nonhomologous end joining complex.

Pathogenic variants in the XRCC4 gene cause short stature with microcephaly and endocrine dysfunction.17,18The clinical features include microcephaly, short stature, hypothyroidism, cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, cardiomyopathy, and later onset ataxia.
The homozygous variant in exon 2 described in the case 10—XRCC4:c.127T > C: p.(Trp43Arg)—has earlier been described in ClinVar as a pathogenic variant.
KS presents with intellectual disability and dysmorphism.
Recently diagnostic criteria for KS have been developed.19
It was ﬁrst described in Japan, but subsequently patients from different countries have been described.

Immune manifestations are seen in around 25% cases and include thrombocytopenia, and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.20 KMT2D gene variants account for over 90% cases of this syndrome.19 Both patients in present report showed heterozygous truncating variants leading to premature truncation of protein.
Eversion of lateral portion of lower eyelids is a characteristic diagnostic feature of KS.
The variant seen in ﬁrst patient of KS is possibly novel variant, KMT2D:c.14890delC(p. Arg4964Valfs(cid:4)30) and not described in ClinVar database.
The variant identiﬁed in the second patient (NM_003482.3: c.11475_11478delACAG:p.

Thus, availability of variety of genetic tests has enabled better identiﬁcation and characterization of patients with short stature seen in the genetic clinic.
NGS helps in diagnosis of most cases of short stature syndromes including NS, KS, and NHS.
Parental testing or sibling testing may be indicated if a variant of unknown signiﬁcance is identiﬁed in cases of heterozygous variants associated with autosomal dominant disorder.
In Xlinked disorder like NHS, the mother may be having minor manifestations that should be carefully looked for like screwdriver incisors as seen in mother of case 9 in present report.

Genes causing short stature include PTPN11, LZTR1, and SOS1 leading to NS.22 Short stature with scoliosis can be caused by ACAN mutations.23 Mutations in ACAN are associated with early onset osteoarthritis.
Missense variants in ARID1B have also been implicated in nonsyndromic short stature.24
Apart from KMT2D that accounts for over 90% cases of KS, KS is also caused by KDM6A and KDM6C heterozygous or hemizygous variants.25
The latter gene causes Xlinked form of the disorder.
In some cases of KS, severe brain malformations can occur like hypogenesis of corpus callosum, hydrocephalus, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, and Dandy–Walker malformation.
Accordingly, skeletal survey, cardiac evaluation, and MRI brain may be indicated in complete evaluation of some of the patients as illustrated in ►Fig.

Conclusions A careful clinical examination with emphasis on clues in the face, eyes, hairs, and teeth along with use of available clinical diagnostic criteria can enable better dysmorphic diagnosis in cases of children with short stature.
An appropriate genetic testing, like MLPA or NGS, can conﬁrm the diagnosis and facilitate better genetic counselling and management.
